beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about Goodhart's Law, when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure, and three questions that test whether a proxy you're tracking still tracks what you actually care about.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: A number on a dashboard climbs every week, and everyone treats that as good news. But a proxy is never the target itself, it's a stand-in, chosen because it used to move together with what you actually care about. Nothing guarantees it still does. The number can keep climbing long after it's stopped meaning what everyone assumes it means.
beats.new_visual_element: A generic dashboard metric panel ticking upward week over week, then an overlay posing the real question: the proxy is up, but is the real target up too?

shot.note: Generic/hypothetical dashboard metric, no real system, company, or vendor named, per FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: Here's the test, before any example: three questions. One, name the target: what's the real thing this number stands in for, and could you actually say it out loud? Two, find the lever: is anyone, or anything, being scored, rewarded, or optimized on this number itself? Three, watch the coupling: has anything changed in how the number gets produced, or who's incentivized by it, since you first started trusting it? A proxy chosen honestly can still go stale, not because it broke, but because something around it changed.
beats.new_visual_element: Checklist card, all 3 tests shown together (Name the Target / Find the Lever / Watch the Coupling)

shot.note: Framework shown fully before any example, matching prior STEM videos' rubric beat.

beats.narration_text: Here's how it actually works. A call center tracks average handle time, how fast each call wraps up, as a stand-in for efficient service. Reward agents for shorter calls, and handle time drops right on schedule. The proxy looks great. But the real target was never short calls, it was problems actually solved. Push handle time down hard enough, and agents start rushing or ending calls early. The number improves. The thing it was supposed to represent gets worse.
beats.new_visual_element: A proxy metric (average handle time) and the real target (problems actually resolved) shown side by side, diverging, tagged DIVERGED

shot.note: [Source: FACTCHECK.md #2/#3 -- generic illustration of a textbook-level, well-documented phenomenon, no real company/vendor named] The proxy, the real target, and the gap between them must all be visible together so the mechanism reads without narration alone.

beats.narration_text: Now the case that would break this test if it were sloppy: the same call center, the same handle-time proxy, under the same pressure to go faster, this time paired with one more number, tracked right alongside it: first-call resolution, whether the problem actually got fixed without a repeat call. Rush a call now, and the repeat-call rate jumps right along with it. The shortcut that used to pay off stops paying off, because the one number it could hide behind is being watched too.
beats.new_visual_element: The same proxy (average handle time) and the same gaming pressure, but now paired with a counterbalancing check (first-call resolution) that is actively tracked alongside it, so the real target stays visible instead of quietly diverging, tagged STAYS HONEST

shot.note: Stress-tests the framework against a naive 'every optimized proxy always diverges' over-trigger. Visually distinct resolution from B04 (STAYS HONEST vs DIVERGED) using the identical gaming pressure, changing only whether a counterbalancing check is being tracked -- per the house falsifiability-stress-test requirement.

beats.narration_text: Here's something to try today, on any system you track. Pick one number you already trust, a dashboard count, a rating, a score. Say out loud what it's actually supposed to stand in for. Then ask: has anything changed about how that number gets produced, or who's rewarded by it, since you started trusting it? If no second number would catch the shortcut, that's worth a closer look, this isn't unique to any one system, it happens anywhere a number gets tracked instead of the thing it was meant to represent.
beats.new_visual_element: The 3 tests restated as a concrete, runnable checklist

shot.note: Concrete action, not a restatement of B03 -- should read as a checklist/task card, not another copy of the framework card.

beats.narration_text: Goodhart's Law isn't about bad metrics. It's about good metrics in changed conditions. A proxy is correlated with the target under the conditions where it was chosen, change the incentive or how it's produced, and it can look just as reliable while quietly stopping being what you wanted.
